https://www.bursa.ro/a-letter-lost-in-a-.text: Our country is in a critical situation, and Sorin Grindeanu, the president of the Chamber of Deputies and, by a happy political coincidence, the president of the Social Democratic Party, yesterday took up the pen to officially announce, through a letter addressed to the leaders of the parliamentary political parties, what Romanians had already found out firsthand: the state has blocked, hospitals no longer have enough people, fuel is getting more expensive, IT systems are crashing, real estate transactions are getting bogged down, and the billions from the PNRR are waiting patiently on the border between promise and impossibility. The situation is serious, but not desperate, because, when institutions no longer function, Romanian politics always has the ultimate solution at hand: the establishment of a committee. Or a committee, as my uncle Iancu would have said. A committee whose head or president would be none other than the "honorable", "esteemed" Sorin Grindeanu. "Romania is going through a period in which the government gridlock is affecting the state's capacity to respond to the country's urgent problems," writes Sorin Grindeanu at the beginning of the letter. An accurate, clear and almost courageous observation, if it did not come from the very center of the political system that produced the gridlock. But let's not be grumbling. The important thing is that the diagnosis has been made. The patient is not responding, the administration's pulse is barely felt, European funding is in the waiting room, but political doctors are still discussing who will occupy the main office and who has the right to hold the stethoscope. The PSD president informs us that "there are essential areas in which the lack of decisions already produces serious effects." In other words, the lack of decisions produces effects, an administrative discovery worthy of being recorded in the Official Gazette. Until now, it was probably believed that indecision is a superior form of prudence, that postponement is a public policy and that a gridlocked government can lead the country through its simple decorative existence. Reality, this eternal opponent of government programs, however, had the impudence to intervene. In support of the above statement, Sorin Grindeanu gives the example of children's hospitals, where the hiring freeze has begun to threaten the functioning of critical departments. "If we do not urgently supplement, through legislative measures, the staffing scheme in Health, the staff shortage in critical areas, the latest example being the ICU Department at Marie Curie Hospital, will lead to the irremediable degradation of hospital services," warns the PSD leader. "Irremediable" is a difficult word, even for a political letter. It means that we are no longer talking about a small budgetary inconvenience, about two signatures lost in a ministerial corridor or about an organizational chart that must be walked from one office to another, but about vital medical services that risk being compromised. Sick children, however, do not know the subtleties of budget balance, they do not know that hiring is blocked in the name of great fiscal principles and they cannot wait for the installation of a Government with full powers. They have this deeply unadministrative impatience to need doctors and nurses right now. The real estate market is not feeling any better either. The platforms of the National Agency for Cadastre and Real Estate Advertising have been affected by cyber attacks, and activity in the field has been blocked. The digitalization of the Romanian state has thus shown its full efficiency: where, in the past, the citizen was stopped by a file with a rail, now he can be stopped instantly by an unavailable computer system. This is progress, without a doubt. The queue at the counter has been replaced by the server error, and the clerk who said "come back tomorrow" has been modernized into an automatic message that no longer specifies when to come back. On top of this technological achievement comes the deadline of July 31. "If we do not adopt a transitional legislative measure by July 31, all real estate transactions will have a 21% VAT rate applied. Which will deepen the crisis in the construction sector," warns Sorin Grindeanu. The deadline was, of course, known, but Romanian politics has a special relationship with the calendar: they ignore it while there are months left, they contest it when there are weeks left, and they declare it a national emergency when there are a few days left. Only then do responsibility, mobilization, and a call to unity appear. If the deadline had been dealt with in advance, the drama would have been lost, and the extraordinary session would have risked becoming a banal one, which, it must be admitted, does not serve anyone from a rhetorical point of view. And fuels are stubbornly increasing in price without waiting for the political crisis to be resolved. "If we do not put the fuel price compensation mechanism back into operation, we will have a new explosion of prices for Romanians," writes the president of the Chamber of Deputies. The explosion is for Romanians, the compensation is for the budget, the explanations are for the press, and the responsibility, being a very sensitive political commodity, is kept in a cool place and away from light. The citizen will pay at the pump the cost of the time lost by those who represent him, but he will be able to have the satisfaction that his price increase was foreseen in an official letter. Faced with these dangers, Sorin Grindeanu proposes "the establishment of a crisis committee at the level of Parliament, formed by representatives of all parliamentary groups". Here, finally, is the solution! When the Government cannot govern, the Parliament will form a committee that will discuss how the Government could be helped to govern without, for the time being, a Government with full powers. It is an institutional architecture of such finesse that only Romanian political practice could conceive it. However, let no one think that it is a committee in the rigid, regulatory and boring sense of the word. Grindeanu clarifies the matter carefully: "I emphasize that this is strictly an informal working group and not a classic parliamentary procedure.” In other words, there is an official crisis, official problems, official deadlines, official billions and official effects on citizens, but the group that will seek solutions will be informal. A happy reconciliation between solemnity and lack of responsibility. If things go well, the committee will be proof of political maturity. If things go badly, it was not even a committee, but only an informal working group, a responsible conversation between concerned people. This group would be "to identify and prepare, on an emergency basis, the amendments and legislative solutions necessary to unblock these situations.” It is comforting to learn that solutions exist and can be identified. All that remains is the small mystery of why they were not identified before the situations needed to be "unblocked.” The fruit of the discussions will form the basis of the "extraordinary session of Parliament that I intend to convene next week," writes Sorin Grindeanu, who, by the way, announced yesterday, in a press conference, that we will have this session on July 27, during which the elected representatives will have to adopt the urgent measures and legislative projects assumed through the PNRR, which, according to the letter, "will bring Romania over 3 billion euros." Three billion euros is, without a doubt, a convincing argument. Not so convincing that the projects would have been adopted on time, but convincing enough to be invoked now, when the need for urgency can be presented as proof of responsibility. From the letter of the President of the Chamber of Deputies, we also note that the said informal committee or group would function "exclusively until the installation of a Government with full powers." Until then, the state will be kept alive by amendments prepared informally and adopted extraordinarily. After the installation of the Government, the committee will be dissolved, the crisis will be declared over, and the parties will resume their usual activity of preventing the next crisis by ignoring its early signs. We have a letter since yesterday. We will have a committee. Then, an extraordinary session. Therefore, the crisis can rest easy: it has entered the parliamentary circuit and, with a little luck, will soon receive a registration number. Articol despre Sorin Grindeanu, lost letter, crisis committee, PNRR.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxe.text: Image caption, The landslide happened at a mine in Policarpa, in the south of the country By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter Latin America online editor Published 20 August 2026, 15:34 BST Updated 3 hours ago At least 13 workers have been killed and another seven injured in a landslide at an unlicensed mine in southern Colombia, local officials say. Witnesses described hearing what they said sounded like an explosion at the open-air artisanal gold mine on Wednesday afternoon, moments before the workers below were trapped. But a local official said the deadly landslide had been caused by the mining work. Emergency workers were able to retrieve the bodies with the help of diggers. Deadly accidents are not uncommon in Colombia, especially at unlicensed mines where locals dig for precious metals without any official oversight. Witnesses said that four of the 13 dead were members of the same indigenous family. Residents of the area said some 50 people, most of them members of the Quillacinga indigenous group, regularly worked in the mine near Policarpa, in southern NariÃ±o province. Between 200,000 and 400,000 people are estimated to engage in artisanal mining in Colombia, with many families relying on the income from selling the precious metals and stones they find to make ends meet. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Hate crime Racial and religious hate crimes at record high in England and Wales, data shows Offences targeting Muslims increased most in 12 months to March – up 15% – while antisemitic hate crimes rose by 10% UK politics live – latest updates Chris Osuh and Aamna Mohdin Thu 8 Oct 2026 08.02 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 08.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK, as the government’s main Islamophobia partner says attacks on mosques are increasing in severity. New Home Office figures show police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132 – while antisemitic hate crimes rose by 10%, from 2,874 to 3,162. The data excluded figures for the Metropolitan police because of a change in their crime recording system. Religious hate crime offences recorded in England and Wales in the 12 months to March – excluding the Met – were at their highest annual total – 8,214 – since records began in 2012. The Home Office reported sharp increases in anti-Muslim offences in September 2025, coinciding with protests and public disorder, and again in March after the outbreak of war between the US and Iran. Anti-Muslim hate crimes reached a record 3,660 offences, the highest annual total since this data was first collected in 2018. The official data comes as The British Muslim Trust (BMT), appointed by the government in July 2025 to monitor anti-Muslim hostility, said there had been a shift from hate aimed at mosques to “targeting [the] Muslims inside”. BMT recorded 78 incidents involving 64 mosques across the UK and the Channel Islands between 21 July 2025 and 30 July 2026, roughly equivalent to an incident every five days. A report published on Thursday by BMT, titled A Year of Division, said: “There has been an unprecedented level of anti-Muslim hate during the last year … The momentum of growing anti-Muslim hostility is driving the attacks against mosques … The defining shift across this reporting period is a movement from hate aimed at the mosque itself to hate targeting Muslims inside it.” View image in fullscreen Supporters of Ukip march in London. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images According to BMT’s own seven-level severity scale, 62.7% of incidents since November 2025 fell into the upper four levels – threats and sustained harassment; weapon present or threats to kill; arson or direct violence; and alleged mass-casualty plots. Between July and October 2025, just 22.2% of incidents were of the more serious kind. BMT added: “Political figures and commentators should take greater care when raising policy concerns regarding immigration or integration. “Rhetoric intended as policy critique on immigration or integration can often become incendiary and difficult to distinguish from hostility directed at British Muslim communities specifically.” Ammer Amin, trustee of Masjid Al-Ummah , a planned mosque on the site of a former church in Watford, which has been repeatedly targeted, said: “It’s almost open season [on Muslims] and people feel emboldened by politicians. “It’s easy to say it’s the Reform party, but it’s not just the Reform party. It’s the Conservative party as well. I’m not party political, but they’re singing from the same hymn sheet. They’re almost competing.” Amin said the mosque’s plans included a sports hall, gym, nursery and food bank for the use of everyone in the local community. In October last year, crucifixes were sprayed on the building’s hoardings. A man later admitted possession of a knife and an axe, but was cleared of criminal damage. In February this year, model pigs were thrown into the premises in another incident. Akeela Ahmed, BMT’s CEO, said: “Security needs are increasing … and many Muslims today are scared to go about their everyday lives. We need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.” Meanwhile, the Community Security Trust has said “antisemitic hate crime remains at an unacceptably high level”. The new government data showed hate crimes against Jewish people were, when data from the Met was excluded, at their second highest level on record. A total of 2,003 offences were recorded, just below the peak of 2,093 in the year ending March 2024, which followed the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza. https://www.journalismpakistan.com/jp-gl.text: JP Global Media Review | October 2026: Press freedom, AI and media survival JournalismPakistan.com | Published: 5 November 2026 | JP Special Report Join our WhatsApp channel October 2026 saw escalating disputes over who controls journalism - from legal battles and government seizures to AI-related content conflicts - while widespread financial strain forced layoffs, restructurings and closures that imperil independent reporting globally. Summary اکتوبر 2026 میں صحافت پر کنٹرول، قانونی تنازعات اور مصنوعی ذہانت کی بحث بڑھی، اور مالی مشکلات نے اداروں میں نوکریاں اور اخباری آپریشن دبا دیے۔ اردو خلاصہ Play Audio Summary Stop October brought renewed confrontations over press freedom, growing legal challenges to government restrictions, expanding disputes over artificial intelligence and mounting financial pressure on news organizations. JournalismPakistan's international coverage documented attacks on journalists, court interventions, newsroom restructuring, surveillance threats, and efforts by publishers to reclaim control over their content. Editor's note October 2026 exposed an increasingly complex struggle over who controls journalism, who can practice it safely and who will pay for its survival. In the United States, the confrontation between President Donald Trump's administration and major news organizations deepened in the courts. In Türkiye, authorities took control of an opposition broadcaster. In Egypt, independent journalists faced allegations of torture, prosecution and imprisonment. Across parts of Asia, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, journalists encountered physical attacks, detention, surveillance and criminal investigations. At the same time, artificial intelligence became a more immediate concern for publishers and broadcasters. European media organizations challenged Meta's proposed terms for using content, a growing international coalition demanded greater transparency and compensation for journalism, and an investigation uncovered an influence operation involving fictitious journalist identities and AI-assisted articles. The economic outlook offered little relief. Newsroom layoffs, proposed restructuring, newspaper closures, and uncertainty over the future of independent digital publications demonstrated that financial instability remains a serious threat to journalism's capacity to serve the public. Yet October also produced important signs of resistance. Courts intervened to protect journalists' access and rights. Publishers challenged technology companies. Press freedom organizations demanded accountability, while professional bodies proposed stronger legal safeguards. The central lesson from October was that journalism faces interconnected threats. Physical violence, legal pressure, technological dependence, and economic weakness may appear to be separate problems, but each can undermine the independence and effectiveness of the news media. Through ongoing international monitoring, JournalismPakistan documented these developments and examined their broader implications for journalism. Introduction October's international media developments extended several major trends identified in September but also revealed how rapidly their consequences were unfolding. The White House press-access dispute, already a defining issue in September, produced new judicial orders, government appeals, allegations of continued exclusion and a broader constitutional challenge. The disagreement raised fundamental questions about whether political authorities can restrict journalists' access because of unfavorable coverage. Elsewhere, criminal laws, national-security provisions and digital regulations became increasingly important instruments affecting journalism. Sudan expanded the scope of a serious national-security offense to include media and electronic publication. Indian publishers challenged data-protection provisions they fear could expose confidential sources. Bangladesh's editors sought judicial safeguards against arbitrary action targeting journalists. The technology debate also intensified. Publishers were no longer simply questioning whether artificial intelligence companies should compensate news organizations. They were organizing international coalitions, seeking injunctions and pursuing competition-law remedies. Throughout October, JournalismPakistan covered 82 international media developments, including follow-up reports on continuing cases. They spanned more than 30 countries and territories across five continents. Taken together, the coverage presented a global media industry confronting political interference, physical danger, legal uncertainty, technological disruption and an increasingly fragile business environment. At a glance Coverage highlights 82 international media reports and developments reviewed More than 30 countries and territories represented Five continents covered Major legal disputes involving press access, source protection, competition and digital regulation Continuing attacks, detentions, prosecutions and threats against journalists Significant developments involving AI, publisher rights, newsroom employment and media ownership Dominant themes Press freedom, journalist safety and accountability Government restrictions and criminal prosecutions Court interventions and legal challenges Artificial intelligence, surveillance and publisher rights Media business, layoffs and newspaper closures Public-service broadcasting and media ownership Cross-border threats and protection of journalists in exile 1. The month in perspective The continuing dispute over White House press access provided one of October's clearest examples of the relationship between government power and independent journalism. On October 5, the White House prevented Politico from completing its scheduled assignment as the primary print-pool reporter aboard Air Force One during President Trump's trip to Nebraska. Other news organizations declined invitations to replace Politico, leaving the traveling press corps without its principal print representative. The confrontation followed earlier restrictions affecting CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. On October 13, US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction protecting their White House access while their constitutional challenge continued. The Trump administration appealed the following day. The dispute did not end there. CNN subsequently accused the White House of continuing to obstruct its presidential travel coverage despite the judicial intervention and warned that further litigation might be necessary. Five television networks: ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, also came under Justice Department antitrust investigation over their collective suspension of White House pool coverage. A separate lawsuit filed on October 26 by six American citizens, represented by the Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic, broadened the debate. The plaintiffs argued that restrictions on journalists' access also infringed the public's constitutional right to receive independent information. These developments transformed an argument over press credentials into a broader dispute involving constitutional protections, government retaliation, collective newsroom action and public access to information. Government control beyond the United States Elsewhere, the pressure took different forms. Turkish authorities appointed a state trustee to pro-opposition broadcaster Halk TV on October 14 following a police raid connected to a corruption investigation involving its chairman, Cafer Mahiroglu. He denied wrongdoing and described the intervention as politically motivated. In Afghanistan, Taliban authorities suspended BBC FM broadcasts nationwide on October 13, citing unspecified repeated violations. The decision further restricted access to independent news in a country where the media already operate under severe constraints. Myanmar's military authorities publicly acknowledged pursuing people associated with five independent media organizations operating in exile through passport cancellations, Interpol procedures and international law-enforcement channels. In Tunisia, prosecutions and restrictions continued to affect independent journalists, while Egypt's authorities pursued cases against independent news outlets and their editors. Although the mechanisms differed, the underlying concern was similar: decisions by governments and state institutions could determine whether journalists were able to report, reach their audiences or continue working. Why it matters: Press freedom is not threatened only when a publication is formally banned. Restrictions on access, control of broadcasters, criminal proceedings and administrative action can weaken independent journalism without eliminating it outright. 2. Press freedom watch October's coverage documented physical attacks, criminal prosecutions, surveillance threats, intimidation and unresolved questions over journalist safety. Killings, assaults and disappearances Bangladeshi journalist Lutfozzaman Fakir Alif was shot dead by motorcycle-borne attackers in Netrokona on October 15. Police initially reported that the attackers' identities and motive were unknown. Investigators later arrested two suspects, with the second placed on three days of police remand. The arrests represented progress in the investigation but did not establish guilt or a motive. In India's Assam state, senior video journalist Sukhendu Rai Choudhury was found dead in a forest on October 16 after going missing 11 days earlier. The circumstances surrounding his death required further investigation. Ugandan television reporter Eria Jengo remained missing more than a month after he was reportedly forced into an unmarked vehicle. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) called on authorities to establish his whereabouts and ensure his safety. In Somalia's Southwest State, the Somali Journalists Syndicate reported that five journalists had fled the region since late August and eight others remained in hiding amid threats and armed conflict. The continuing insecurity extended to journalists covering public protests and elections. Two Serbian journalists, Mihajlo Stojković and Jelena Stojković, were assaulted while investigating allegations of electoral irregularities near Vranje on October 25. In Albania, three media workers required hospital treatment following alleged police assaults during protests in Tirana. In France, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) documented around 30 journalists assaulted or obstructed while covering demonstrations, with incidents involving police, protesters and other individuals. A Euronews crew was attacked in Paris while filming looting. Although its camera was recovered, the memory card containing recorded footage was missing. In India, nearly three dozen journalists were detained while covering protests in New Delhi, Reuters reported on October 12. Some detentions occurred after the Supreme Court had intervened to protect journalists' ability to work. The incidents illustrated the difficulty of exercising press freedom during politically sensitive events, even where formal legal protections exist. The occupied West Bank and cross-border threats Journalists covering the occupied West Bank continued facing violence and obstruction. Armed Israeli settlers assaulted AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh near Aqraba on October 6 and stole his camera equipment. Later in the month, Israeli police investigated attacks involving Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine. CPJ separately reported that Israeli forces detained journalists, raided Al-Ghad TV's offices and fired tear gas toward reporters during operations in Hebron. Another settler attack near Umm Al-Khair on October 28 was followed by the detention of journalists Andrey Khrzhanovskiy and Jasper Nathaniel. Freelance journalist Adele Shoko was also assaulted, according to CPJ. These incidents raised continuing questions about the safety of reporters covering violence, military operations and civilian communities under occupation. Threats also crossed national borders. In Britain, three Iranian nationals went on trial over allegations that they conducted surveillance of Iran International journalists to assist preparations for serious violence. All three denied the charges. In the United States, CPJ condemned the publication of private information targeting exiled Iranian investigative journalist Mohammad Jorjandi and his family. The organization said it was investigating the harassment, while the identity of those responsible remained unestablished. Journalists forced into exile may therefore remain vulnerable to intimidation, surveillance and coercion beyond the countries they left. Criminal cases and imprisonment Egypt produced some of October's most serious press freedom developments. Six journalists associated with the independent Matsadaash platform alleged that they had been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions while in detention. Their lawyers entered the allegations into the official investigation record. Separately, Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was questioned and released on bail on October 21 in a case concerning the outlet's operations and reporting. On October 27, an Egyptian court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds, ordered the website closed and its property confiscated, and took her into custody. The sequence demonstrated how release in one proceeding did not necessarily remove the risk posed by separate legal action. In Tunisia, journalist Zied el-Heni received a four-year prison sentence on terrorism-related charges connected to leaked audio recordings he had reported on. In Georgia, Formula TV anchor Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 30 days of administrative detention over social media posts deemed insulting to senior politicians. Iranian journalists Artin Ghazanfari and Omid Faraghat received lengthy prison sentences under espionage legislation, prompting CPJ to demand that their convictions be overturned. In Bangladesh, three jailed journalists remained under investigation in a crimes against humanity case involving allegedly provocative media statements during the July 2024 uprising. Investigators were given until January 2027 to complete their report. The cases involved different legal systems and allegations, but collectively emphasized the growing importance of criminal proceedings in determining journalists' professional freedom and personal security. Why it matters: Attacks on journalists have immediate consequences for those involved, but their wider effect can be equally damaging. Violence, prosecution and intimidation can discourage investigation, limit access to sources and leave communities without reliable information. 3. Courts, laws and regulatory pressure October highlighted the increasingly influential role of courts in defining the boundaries of journalism. Laws affecting reporting and confidential sources In Sudan, Temporary Decree No. 7 of 2026 amended Article 51 of the Criminal Code to explicitly cover certain support for acts of war against the state expressed through media and electronic publishing. The provision already carried penalties that could include death or life imprisonment. The amendment did not introduce those punishments but expanded the stated means through which the existing offense could be committed. Its potential application to journalism and online commentary raised serious concerns about the scope of national-security legislation. Another Sudanese journalist, Rasha Hassan, was detained following a defamation complaint over a Facebook repost concerning allegations that pupils had been excluded from examinations for unpaid fees. In India, 21 major news publishers challenged provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in the Supreme Court. They argued

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve View image in fullscreen Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve The age of extinction Illegal wildlife trade Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Supported by About this content Rebecca Ratcliffe Thu 19 Nov 2026 06.03 EST Last modified on Thu 19 Nov 2026 06.05 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa , on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions. The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer. The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago , when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park , owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea. The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy , but later allowed to go ahead. Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.” Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them. “As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said. The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres. Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them. “A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.” Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit. The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.” Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants. The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter. A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
